articles.text: The Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail project has attracted a significant number of bids for a project of its modest size. The City’s proposed project to install a handrail and build steps on the hill between the Community Hall and Guilford Road has attracted an unusually large number of bids from contractors interested in doing the work, according to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. A bid opening was held on October 6, with eight bidders showing interest in the project. “Contractors appear to be looking for work,” Gonzales noted at a Park Commission meeting on October 6. Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent agreed, adding that the city used an electronic virtual bid submittal, which may have boosted the response. “It’s wonderful to have eight bids. That means there is a lot of interest and that it is a competitive [process],” she said. “We had a Zoom bid opening, when usually our bid openings are in person.” Bids were received from HM Construction, Inc., Sposeto Engineering, Inc., FBD Vanguard Construction, Inc., Bay Construction Co., Wickman Development & Construction, Valentine Corporation, Kerex Engineering, Inc., and CF Contracting. The Highland-Guilford Steps are located on the southern entrance to the Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park and provide access to the Tea House. The existing configuration of the pedestrian pathway does not meet the City’s building code or Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements for exterior steps. City Administrator Sara Lillevand told City Council at a September 7 meeting that city staff had received a report of a trip and fall that occurred on the stairs, elevating the project’s priority. The engineer’s estimate for the total cost of the project is $155,000. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club raised funds for the project with a combined donation of $55,000. The city will place emphasis on improving pedestrian safety, which includes reconfiguring colored concrete steps and landings with a nonslip finish; decorative handrails on both sides of the steps and landings; and replacing the sloped landing at the entrance off Highland Avenue with a small pedestrian plaza. Native shrub plantings around the plaza may include coffeeberry and Ribes Sanguineum, and a grove of native oaks will replace a dying, mature oak. Once the bidding process is finalized, City staff will bring a recommendation to City Council for review. The project will begin after City Council approves a contractor. “Any time there’s a bid opening, that is always exciting to me. Capital project delivery is one of the great things we do in Public Works,” Gonzales said.
articles.title: Highland-Guilford Steps and Handrail Project attracts large number of bids

articles.text: The League of Women Voters hosted a town hall-style virtual meeting on October 5 to discuss Piedmont’s Housing Element and housing needs. Guest speakers included Rani Batra, Chair of Piedmont’s Housing Advisory Committee, Melissa Breach, Chief Operating Officer of California YIMBY (Yes In My Backyard), and Gloria Bruce, Executive Director of East Bay Housing Organizations. The discussion included a presentation on the state’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation. The Housing Element is a mandatory part of the Piedmont’s General Plan and, by State law, must be updated every eight years. The Element must address Piedmont’s immediate and longterm housing needs and set forth the City’s goals, policies, and actions to support increased housing. To help guide the process, the City convened a Housing Advisory Committee comprised of Piedmont citizens. In introductory remarks, Breach noted that California still has 25% of the homeless population in the U.S., while only having 12% of the nation’s population. California’s housing crisis is the catalyst for legislation that aims to increase the state’s housing stock and diminish its large homeless population. “The governor has already signed 37 housing bills, which is incredibly exciting,” Breach said. “Funds have been set aside for affordable housing. [It is] an unprecedented amount, but not nearly as much as we need.” YIMBY was the lead advocate on State Senate Bill 9, and the lead sponsor of SB 10, both signed by Gov. Newsom this year. The League of Women Voters endorsed both bills. SB 9 allows for duplexes and lot-splits in California, legislations Breach defined as “the bill that ended single-family zoning in California.” SB 10 allows for local governments to streamline and avoid red-tape requirements for new housing. Batra addressed the city’s process of meeting its goals of 587 new housing units in the upcoming Regional plan. “Our job is to identify land and sites to accommodate the RHNA. That doesn’t mean the city is responsible for building the housing itself, but [the city] needs to pave the way for that production to occur,” she said. Batra said the allocation represents “the magnitude of the challenge and opportunity, and the level of creativity and change that we may need to undertake to achieve this.” The city will invite the public to attend a Housing Element Community Workshop on December 2. articles.text: Governor Gavin Newsom’s California Comeback Plan includes a $15 billion investment in our climate -- with $3.9 billion going towards Zero-Emission Vehicles (ZEVs). This comes one year after the Governor’s Executive Order that 100 percent of in-state sales of new passenger cars and trucks will be zero-emission by 2035. What does this mean for Piedmonters and the city’s climate action goals? Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, adopted in 2018, outlines a target of 50% ZEV ownership by 2030. According to 2019 vehicle registration data, about 7% of vehicles registered in Piedmont are ZEVs. When ZEVs are charged using East Bay Community Energy’s Renewable 100 plan, vehicles can run on 100% California solar & wind energy rather than fossil fuels. Not only do electric vehicles benefit the environment and advance Piedmont and California’s climate action goals, but they also make sense economically. Tools like Plug In America’s PlugStar incentive search, the California Air Resources Board’s DriveClean incentive search, or Veloz’s Electric For All campaign Incentive assistant can help Piedmonters research and discover which incentives they qualify for. Some of these incentives include up to $7,500 in Federal Tax Credits, $4,500 from the California Clean Vehicle Rebate Project, $1,500 from the California Vehicle Retirement Consumer Assistance Program, $1,500 from the California Clean Fuel Reward, $9,500 from Bay Area Clean Cars for All, and preferred pricing from Drive Clean Bay Area’s EV Discount Campaign. Other incentives include an Alternative Fuel Infrastructure Tax Credit for those who purchase residential fueling equipment, EV use of HOV lanes, and clean air vehicle discounts on Bay Area Bridges. In addition to point-of-sale discounts, rebates, and incentives, EVs are known for their capacity to save money over time. Energy.gov uses a tool called the eGallon, showing how much cheaper it is to drive on electricity, while FuelEconomy.gov provides a tool to directly compare fuel costs between vehicles, and PG&E provides an EV Savings Calculator which calculates the cost of specific electric vehicles to own over 5 years, including the cost of the vehicle, electricity vs gasoline, maintenance, and insurance. As part of Piedmont’s climate action goals, the City is having important conversations around EV Charging Stations in the Civic Center Area and Fleet Electrification. Piedmont would be following in the footsteps of the state of Washington and Bay Area cities like Fremont, San Francisco, and Sacramento which have made progress in purchasing EVs as part of a municipal fleet electrification process. While Piedmonters can currently add a Level 2 charging system to their home through a streamlined permit process, adding public charging stations in the City could provide an incentive to adopt electric vehicles by providing additional opportunities to charge them quickly. While ZEVs are just one step towards meeting Piedmont and California’s climate action goals, investing in an electric vehicle is an important step to investing in our climate and our future. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: In the last three weeks Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign has held three events demonstrating the depth and breadth of support for Piedmont schools. Parties celebrating new community members, major donors, and Piedmont schools’ alumni brought together a large number of supporters. On September 20, the Education Foundation hosted an event outside Piedmont Community Hall to welcome new families to town. Giving Campaign donor Xenia Meyer moved here with her family a year and a half ago. “The community here is so welcoming to newcomers,” she said. “The whole ethos of ‘it takes a village’ is something I really feel here.” Cortney and Ben Allen hosted an event in their backyard on Sheridan Avenue on September 29 to celebrate families providing significant levels of support for Piedmont schools. “It was so nice to gather in person and have great conversations with parents,” said hostess Cortney Allen. “It was a beautiful night with a wonderful group of community members,” On Thursday, October 7, Alicia and Jim Kalamas on Bellevue Avenue hosted the newly formed Alumni Committee with 80 Piedmont alumni. More than 400 Piedmont residents are alumni of the schools and have returned to raise their own families here. With a total of $1.4 million raised thus far, the Giving Campaign is almost halfway to this year’s goal of raising $3 million to support students and the schools. The funds raised by the Giving Campaign will help close the gap between what the schools receive from state, federal, and local taxes and what it costs to provide an excellent education. The gap is approximately $2,140 per student. Giving Campaign funds help preserve small class sizes, elective and AP classes, music and art programs, librarians, counselors, class aides, and other specialists. The Ed Foundation accepts pledges with monthly payments, by credit card or through online bill pay, as well as gifts of stock and from Donor Advised Funds. PEF’s tax ID is 94-6426176, checks can be made payable to Piedmont Education Foundation and sent to 401 Highland Avenue, and credit card contributions can be made by phone at 653-1816 or online at PiedmontEdFoundation. Pictured are Alicia Gruber Kalamas (left), Ashley Stevanovic, Sarah Meyjes, Peter Wagener, Jill Saper, and Amelie Kappes. org/donate .

articles.text: Fall is a time for transitions. School is underway, but as the darkness comes earlier and the air gets colder, it seems like something shifts in our family life. We are spending less time playing outdoors, more time looking for indoor activities, and the routine of day to day becomes our guiding force. I find this shift fascinating because it always takes me by surprise – at least a little bit. I wake up one day and realize that summer is over, even though I have known this for weeks. Obviously, the holidays coming up are part of this transition, but I’m interested in spending more time thinking about the “in between” – the days when it’s not about costumes and trick or treating, but remembering the cleats on the way to soccer practice. It’s not about the big family meal with turkey, but the grilled cheese sandwiches on a Tuesday. Not the days with tons of presents, but packages that bring a new fleece to keep warm on the walk to school in the morning. How do we make sure that the “in between” days have opportunities for growth and excitement in our family? It’s so easy to get caught in the routine of daily tasks. I’d like to propose that this time of year is the perfect opportunity to use creativity to imagine with your family what is possible. What does exquisite look like for your family life? In the book Play – How it Shapes the Brain, Opens the Imagination, and Invigorates the Soul, Dr. Stuart Brown and Christopher Vaughan write eloquently about the importance Using creativity to make the most of “in-between” days. of Creative Play. “Creative Play takes our minds to places we have never been, pioneering new paths that the real world can follow.” (pg. 93) How can we use Creative Play to dream with our kids? Here is one idea, but I bet you can put on your creative hats and come up with tons more! Family Vision Board In the olden days, we used to make vision boards with these things called magazines, but your children likely have never experienced an actual magazine. So, for the purposes of this activity, ye old internet and a printer will work just fine. Get a big piece of poster board and divide it into four sections. Label each section: Daily Life, Play Together, Play Apart, Big Dreams. Before you start, help everyone get in a playful mindset by playing a silly game like twister or Hokie Pokie or Freeze Dance. Now, with laptop available, start asking your kids and all adults in the house, “What would our days look like if our daily life was truly exquisite?” Let everyone throw ideas out there and then google images that match the ideas. Print them out and paste them on the board. Repeat with: “How do we all want to play together?” “How do we want to play individually? “What big dreams do we have that may feel out of reach right now, but might be fun or exciting some day for our family?” I hope you enjoy the “in between” days and use all of that creative energy to make every day enjoyable...and a few of them memorable! articles.text: Artist Karima Cammell founded and teaches “Castle in the Air” after-school art classes for Piedmont kids at all three elementary schools. When not teaching youngsters, she paints. Her current exhibit, “High Water,” is on view at Holton Studio Gallery. 2100 Fifth Street, in Berkeley until October 30. The show opened with a reception on October 9 and includes Cammell’s thought-provoking paintings. Her art scans the shore, finding a world both on fire and drowning beneath waves of social, political, and climate change. Cammell is well known for being the founder of beloved Fourth Street shop Castle in the Air in Berkeley but since closing the store has pivoted to being a full-time artist. She also continues her work as a children’s author and illustrator and runs the ever popular art classes for Piedmont youth. Along with artist Ben Yates, Cammell teaches classes ranging in subjects from calligraphy to watercolor to miniature food sculpture. “Our after-school program is great fun,” Cammell said. “We teach kids calligraphy, watercolors, simple bookbinding and illumination. We operate on the value that art is a gift, and it makes our work infinitely rewarding.” To see the after-school class offerings, see Homeroom.com. Classes are open now and will return in the Winter and Spring of 2022. To learn more about the show, see Castleintheair. biz/highwater. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. The film recreated convincingly the high-wire action playing out under the tower of a muddy, dangerous project, a quagmire showing frighteningly primitive engineering feats (1886-1889). The viewer already likely knows that a French competition for a monument to promote the Paris World’s Fair was afoot, and Gustave Eiffel won. The construction hit troubled waters, and public opinion turned against Eiffel who was the face of the “metal folly.” Parisians genuinely feared it would topple and come crashing down on them. A romantic plotline that people believe is the lore for the tower’s sweeping, cursive “A” shape is an homage to Adrienne, his teenage lover. It is best to not examine the legend too closely for fact. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team shocked everyone but itself, claiming its first victory of the season last Friday, October 8 in Berkeley, 28-26, and spoiling the Yellowjackets’ homecoming game. “It was a very emotional win; we persevered,” exclaimed coach Jerome Johnson. “The boys hung in there and it was a battle. They never quit when we were down. I’m so proud of them.” It was perhaps the most hostile home crowd in Piedmont football’s recent memory, with Berkeley students ridiculing the visiting town’s affluent reputation, chanting “Daddy’s money!” throughout the entire game. But you could have heard a pin drop in the home stands when the game concluded. The only voices ringing throughout Berkeley High stadium were Piedmont players and fans, and coaches who have been grappling with a roster of only 16-18 players since the start of the season. The win featured senior Adhi Bornstein in his first game starting at quarterback. He led the team on its game-winning drive after gaining possession of the ball with 2:41 left in the game. He finished with 261 passing yards, three passing touchdowns and a rushing score. articles.text: Six miles of hiking on Hayward Plunge and Greenbelt trails Halloween is right around the corner, so what better time to delve into the spooky and haunted. Growing up around Hayward, the gruesome legend of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park is a well-known story, which provides an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class of students up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night, when the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or crying, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in white garb when he was a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be protected by thickets of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for Eucalyptus trees tower overhead. Travel up the stairs and stay next to Ward Creek to continue on the Hayward Plunge Trail. The hilly trail provides over 1,100 feet in elevation gain in six miles. A view of the Greenbelt Trail alongside Ward Creek, which connects with the Hayward Plunge Trail.

Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them—sometimes laughter or crying, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children in white garb when he was a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be protected by thickets of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep downhill declines. It is considered a very technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for Staff Photos A spillway along Ward Creek on the Hayward Plunge Trail, a notoriously haunted park in the East Bay. Eucalyptus trees tower overhead. Travel up the stairs and stay next to Ward Creek to continue on the Hayward Plunge Trail. The trail is popular for mountain bikers. With quick ascents and declines. another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree line, and you’ll have the option to head back down, or turn right and walk down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail where you’ll be reunited with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles, we only passed 29 people at noon on a Sunday. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought the feeling that eyes were always following. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive. The hilly trail provides over 1,100 feet in elevation gain in six miles. Hikers will cross numerous bridges on the hike. articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Father/Daughter will premiere starting November 12 for one month and will be available to stream December 7 through 12. Father/Daughter, by playwright Kait Kerrigan and directed by M. Graham Smith, is a contemporary romance featuring two actors playing two pairs of lovers. The structurally incentive play details how parents and children can impact romantic lives. Father/Daughter is the recipient of the Edgerton Foundation New Play Award, which allows productions time for development and rehearsal through a monetary grant. Kerrigan, an award-winning playwright and lyricist, is best-known for We Have to Hold Hands and Mad Ones. “Kait Kerrigan’s writing is insightful, audacious, and liable to make you either laugh or cry when you least expect it,” said Artistic Director Josh Costello. To purchase tickets for live performances, or for streaming access, visit https://www. auroratheatre.org/fatherdaughter Photo by David Allen The play Father/Daughter by Kait Kerrigan will open at Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley on November 12. ®

articles.text: Michael Morgan Oakland Symphony will honor the late Michael Morgan, its conductor for 30 years, with an all-star memorial concert at the Paramount Theater on Tuesday, October 19, at 6:30 p.m. Artists from across the Bay Area and throughout the U.S. will join in celebrating the life and legacy of Maestro Morgan. The San Francisco Conservatory of Music, San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the Oakland Ballet, Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, Mads Tolling, Zachary Gordon, and many more will be present. Morgan was also music director of the Sacramento Philharmonic Orchestra and artistic director of Festival Opera in Walnut Creek. As a guest conductor, he appeared with most of the country’s major orchestras including the New York Philharmonic, New York City Opera, Photo by Liz Hafalia, San Francisco Chronicle San Francisco Opera, and more. Morgan passed away on August 20 at age 63. The concert is free to the public, but you must RSVP before Tuesday, October 19. Proof of vaccination is required to enter the Paramount Theatre. Masks must be worn while seated. Children under 12 are not permitted to attend. RSVP by visiting https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/event/ we-remember-michael/.

articles.text: San Francisco Conservatory of Music (SFCM) will present a baroque orchestral performance on Halloween, October 31, at 2 p.m. The concert will be held at the Caroline H. Hume Concert Hall and will be live-streamed. Pieces from some of the most iconic baroque composers will be performed, including the music of Antonio Vivaldi, Arcangelo Corelli, Henry Purcell, Andre Cardinal Destouches and Johann Sebastian Bach. Special guests include dancer Jennifer Meller, baroque oboist Marc Schachman, and soprano Jayne Diliberto. Corey Jamason and Elisabeth Reed serve as co-directors for the baroque ensemble. The Conservatory’s baroque ensemble performs music of the 17th and 18th centuries in both orchestral and chamber settings. Nearly all instruments and voice types can participate in this genre. Many pieces have been performed by the ensemble in the recent past, including Handel’s Ode for St. Cecelia, Semele, Serse, Rinaldo, Giulio Cesare, Ariodante, Rodelinda, Atalanta, Agrippina, Alcina, Monteverdi’s L’incoronazione di Poppea, Purcell’s The Fairy Queen and Charpentier’s Les arts florrisants. The ensemble has also participated in the premieres of new works by composition faculty members Mason Bates and Elinor Armer. Tickets for the in-person or livestream may be purchased at https://sfcm.edu/performance-calendar/event/sfcm-baroque-orchestra. Proof of vaccination is required to enter SF Conservatory.

articles.text: The film The Revenant is an extraordinary film: intense, unrelenting, gorgeous to behold and unflinching in its realism. The year is 1823. It’s mid-winter in Montana and South Dakota. A group of men, working for The Rocky Mountain Fur Company, are just completing six months of trapping, preparing pelts and readying their riverboat for a return trip to their base camp, a roughly constructed fort downstream. The trip will be long and arduous. The forest is quiet, wind stirs high in the trees when suddenly a man, in mid-sentence, is shot in the throat by an arrow. The group is set upon by Arikara warriors, and the trappers must fight a desperate and brutal battle as they attempt to get to the boat and escape. Among the few survivors are Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his son, Hawk (Forrest Goodluck), who is part Pawnee. During one of their stops along the way Glass is attacked by a grizzly sow, protecting her cubs. It is one of the most heart-stopping scenes in the film, a mauling that leaves Glass close to death. The party makes the decision to leave behind three men, including Hawk, to bury Glass when he dies (they are certain he is near death) and then make the journey on their own to the fort. His son is killed by one of the trappers, but Glass, still alive, is thrown into a shallow grave and partially buried. Through sheer will, he eventually emerges, discovers the body of his dead son, A scene from Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu’s The Revenant. Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible, John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – which will take your breath away – and the crucible of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (Birdman), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so, the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. The acting is superb; it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they endured as they went through a long and grueling shoot. They, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, were recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The Revenant. Directed by Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Tom Hardy, Domhall Gleeson. 2 hrs., 36 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Nicholas Hoult protrays J.R.R. Tolkien in Tolkien. There are three narrative threads that run through Tolkien, a lush production told under the umbrella of what is loosely referred to as a biopic. At the outset, the film tells the story of a band of four young brothers, mates at an English prep school, who spend hours in each other’s company while insisting that art can and will change the world. There is Geoffrey (Anthony Boyle), Christopher (Tom Glynn-Carney), Robert (Patrick Gibson) and, of course, Tolkien (Nicholas Hoult), who is more formally known as John Ronald Reuel (J.R.R.). While their friendship is interesting and perhaps an accurate portrayal, there is also a restrained, cerebral quality to their interactions. Something is missing. Perhaps an intensity. The second thread is the meeting of Tolkien and Edith Bratt. Their encounter initially takes place in a rooming house for foster children, she as a companion to the wealthy owner of the home. He is brought there when, at 12-years-old, his mother unexpectedly dies of diabetes. His lodging is arranged by his mentor and guardian, Father Frances (Colin Meaney), who promises to assist the boy as best he can. Gradually, over a period of years, Edith and Tolkien are drawn to one another and their connection grows. But their attraction and relationship is described, like so much of this story, with caution. They are young, and there are embers waiting to be fanned. The third thread, and one that is ripe with graphic details and information, is the rich imagination of Tolkien. He fills the walls of his rooms with his drawings. He keeps notebooks filled with his stories. And he demonstrates a passion for language. In one remarkable scene he sits in a restaurant with Edith and they have a conversation about a phrase, much loved by Tolkien, “cellar door.” Of all the exposition in the film, there is something captivating in this moment. Eventually, he meets a university professor, a scholar of philology, who points the way. Unfortunately, it is Tolkien’s imagination that seems too quickly to be passed over. In scenes that are filled with his drawings, the camera never pauses to reveal in close-up the intricacies of his fabulist talent and the richness of a world beyond. Behold, there are dragons, gnarled trees, characters. Unexpectedly, it becomes evident that the story is a series of long flashbacks, revealed from the point of view of Tolkien, an army officer trapped in one of the unspeakable warren trenches of WWI and struggling to survive. So harrowing are the scenes of war, so overwhelming with danger and perpetual carnage, Tolkien retreats into memory or fantasy. The Germans with flamethrowers become dragons bellowing long streams of fire; tanks are knights on horseback riding slowly through a wasted killing field; black, wispy battlefield smoke becomes ominous and threatening. Actually, Tolkien’s experience in that hellish war, more specifically the Battle of the Somme, could not only have been the fulcrum for this film, but it could have been the gateway to the years ahead when he actually imagined and then crafted The Hobbit and later The Lord of the Rings, which taken together represent some of the most imaginative writing of the 20th century. Regrettably, Tolkien ends just as J.R.R. sits down at his desk and gazes out a window at a bucolic field in the distance and writes just two words: The Hobbit. Tolkien. Directed by Dome Karukoski. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Lily Collins, Colm Meaney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Tolkien a fascinating history of JRR Tolkien

What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – which will take your breath away – and the crucible of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (Birdman), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so, the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. The acting is superb; it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they endured as they went through a long and grueling shoot. They, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, were recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The Revenant. Directed by Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Tom Hardy, Domhall Gleeson. 2 hrs., 36 min. Rated R. ADVERTISE IN THE POST

It’s also an amazing technical achievement, created by some 40 animators, working with stop-motion claymation, real props, three dimensional sets, with a cast of chickens with perky dialogue and personalities to match. The story is set on a bleak chicken farm in Yorkshire, England, run by a cranky (bordering on sadistic) commandant, Mrs. Tweedy (Miranda Richardson). She rants and screeches about the lack of egg production and is working on a Rube Goldberg plan to turn all the chickens into pot pies if things don’t pick up. Among the chickens is Ginger (Julia Sawahla), a spunky prize hen, who is not about to simply give in to Mrs. Tweedy, unlike her complacent peers. Early on, she tries to dig a tunnel under the wire fence using a kitchen fork and is caught by Mrs. Tweedy’s guard dogs and put into solitary confinement. All seems lost, the chickens’ fate all but sealed, when Rocky, a Rhode Island circus rooster, who can fly, and is a Yank to boot, shows up. Brash, overly confident, he convinces the hens that he can teach them to fly as well. Of course, Rocky also falls for Ginger, and as a result the two begin to hatch a plan for a prison-break. Surprisingly Rocky does need some convincing. Meanwhile, Mrs. Tweedy’s potpie contraption is coming together, egg production is declining, and both Rocky and Ginger realize that time is of the essence – all the hens have all been put on double rations in order to fatten them up. articles.text: Kids will love Wallace & Gromit, an Oscar-winning franchise of 30-minute shorts, plus one feature. The first short was A Grand Day, followed by The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave, and A Matter of Loaf and Death. The Curse of the Were-Rabbit was the Aardman studio’s first Claymation feature film. The stars of the franchise are, of course, Wallace (Peter Sallis), a suburban Brit with a pearshaped head and wide, ear-to-ear smile, and his faithful, industrious, ever-silent Beagle (graduate of the Dogwart Academy). They live together in a house filled with labor saving inventions and Rube Goldberg-like contraptions, invented by Wallace, whose day jobs include window cleaner, and baker. In Were-Rabbit, he is the owner of the Anti-Pesto Services, a pest control company. His current responsibility is to keep the village gardens free of vegetable-eating rabbits. He, of course, has an invention just for this purpose, a vacuum that sucks up the rabbits, which he keeps in his basement. All of this is in preparation for the Town’s annual vegetable growing competition, the winning prize being a golden carrot. One evening, using his invention, Wallace captures a rabbit who is eating Lady Tottington’s (Helena Bonham Carter) vegies. Unfortunately, his contraption has a miscalculation, and he creates a gigantic Were-Rabbit that is ravenous for vegetables, and is chomping its way through garden after village garden, something that will surely upset the coming vegie growing contest. Hearing of this garden emergency, Lord Victor Quartermaine (Ralph Fiennes) volunteers to hunt down the culprit with his rifle and shoot it; however, lady Tottington objects, and convinces the town folk to allow Wallace and his Anti-Pesto Services to take care of the problem. The mystery that Wallace must solve is who or what is this Were-Rabbit? It’s a puzzle that takes Wallace and Gromit on an adventure. Wallace even discovers giant muddy footprints that lead into his own house. And even Gromit, who is highly intelligent, can’t figure out the source of the footprints. There are lots of surprises and chases, and even threats by Quartermaine to kill the Were-Rabbit with a golden bullet. Things get more than a bit chaotic, at one point involving an airborne dogfight between Gromit and Q.’s dog, Phillip. There’s a bit of romance-lite thrown in (Wallace and Lady T. have some chemistry). It’s all daffy fun, wonderfully creative, involving lots of pratfalls and puns. Youngsters will be smitten. Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. Directed by Nick Park. Claymation by Aardman Animations. With voices of Peter Sallis, Ralph Fiennes, Helena Bonham-Carter. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated G.

articles.text: Pianist Adrien Zarragoza Solano Symphony music director and conductor Semyon Lohss is an inspiration. He is all for the music and the results show it. Under his direction the orchestra plays with razor sharp precision and with great attention to dynamics. The orchestra was featured in Schubert‘s 6th Symphony. It was a very Viennese interpretation, and the quick tempos kept the orchestra on its toes. Many years ago, friends of mine who played in the San Francisco Symphony under Pierre Monteux said that he inspired the orchestra to play above their abilities. That’s what Semyon Lohss does. We have a great composer in our midst. You probably don’t know his name as a prominent musician. His credentials are impressive. Among them are that he was a violinist in the Amsterdam Philharmonic and Director of the youth program with the San Francisco Symphony. He is now a State Farm insurance agent, but Frank Bliss is a great composer. Frank’s newest work is a four-movement symphony based on the business cycle. What a novel concept that is. Now that I have got your attention… Munich, Germany hosts the world’s largest folk festival – the Oktober Bierfest. For the second year in a row, this gigantic festival was canceled. Piedmont made up for it… More specifically the Piedmont Center for the Arts. You don’t have to fly to Germany or even speak German. Admission to the 9th annual Piedmont Beer Festival was $10 per person and included a custom pilsner glass with the Center’s logo. For an additional five dollars you could get an authentic German meal of grilled Bratwurst, warm potato salad and warm red cabbage, all courtesy of Piedmont Grocery. To say this is a popular event is putting it mildly. Approximately 150 beer connoisseurs and German food lovers enjoyed themselves immensely. This year the celebrity judges included Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery’s Dave Larson. Fire chief Dave Brannigan was on hand to check the results. That was on Friday. Next year, let’s have a German-style oompah band. And now some musical notes... On the local music scene, the Prometheus Symphony played a virtual concert. Their programs are always interesting, and we look forward to live concerts in the near future. The Solano Symphony is another fine local orchestra. They opened their 35th season on Sunday with a very exciting concert. Adrien Zarragoza was the featured soloist in Beethoven’s Piano Concerto #3. This young pianist is a talent to watch. He has a blazing temperament which was perfect for the Beethoven concerto. In many ways Zaragoza reminds me of a young Vladimir Horowitz. His technique is facile; he can thunder with the best of pianists, and then in an instant caress the keys in the most gentle manner. As I said, he is a talent to watch. articles.text: Book lovers with the First Mondays Reading Group included Alicia Rivera, Ken Young, Mike Henn, Albert Chen, Nancy Henn, Swee Ling Chen, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long The First Monday Reading Group met 14 strong at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on October 4. a lovely, warm day. The early fall, “secret summer” day and beautiful location and refreshments may have been incentives for readers come for the discussion, but the expectation of an interesting discussion of the group’s October book, the best-seller Nomadland, was an even stronger motivation. Nomadland: Surviving America in the Twenty-First Century is a 2017 nonfiction book by American journalist Jessica Bruder. This is her account of older Americans who, after the recession from 2007 to 2009, have adopted transient lifestyles going from one place to another around the United States in search of low-paying, seasonal jobs. The book was adapted to the 2020 film of the same name, starring Frances McDormand, which won the Academy Award for that year’s Best Picture. Bruder expanded a cover story for Harper’s magazine into Nomadland. Her nomads, many of whom are senior citizens, don’t think of themselves as “homeless.” Instead, they refer to themselves as “houseless.” They feel they are no longer burdened by mortgage payments, repairs, and other house expenses. However, most of them did not become “houseless” by choice; many lost their houses because of mortgage fraud, job loss, health care debt, divorce, alcoholism, and additional factors. They sleep in their cars, trucks, or campers and try to make the best of their situations. The author traveled with some of the houseless for years while researching and writing her book. She built her novel around a senior citizen named Linda May. She and her fellow travelers found physically demanding, low-wage jobs in North Dakota sugar beet fields, California campgrounds, and an Amazon distribution center in Texas. These seniors created community wherever they were; offering tips for overcoming common troubles, sharing food, repairing vehicles, helping each other through depression, and sharing information about potential employers. The readers felt that the book was helpful in making people more conscious of the hardships that lower income, older adults face in America. These are not people that Piedmonters usually see in their daily experiences. The severity of what some seniors in our nation experience was a cause for not only disappointment, but also anger for some readers. The fact that these people are living as nomads was seen as a result of our country’s move away from its past, three-legged retirement planning model. Retirement income for Americans was once composed of Social Security, pensions, and personal savings; but for these nomads there is now only Social Security, which does not provide enough income to have a house. During their prior lives the Nomadland seniors worked in many, different jobs with low wages and no pensions. They had little or no money to invest in personal 401K plans that were supposed to be pension replacements, and there was little for personal savings either. They were in precarious situations and when a personal problem or the national financial disaster of the 2008 recession happened, they were pushed over the edge and became houseless. It was noted that the low levels of savings that many people were accumulating for their retirements was evident many years ago; so the difficult situations of many seniors should not have been a surprise today. However, it was also noted that our country does not seem to address distant, long-term problems particularly well. Climate change was seen as another example of this. Readers’ disappointment and anger were directed at companies like Amazon, and the harsh working conditions they impose on their employees. The huge disparity in income and wealth between the corporate “one tenth of one percent” elites, like Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, and Bruder’s low income, hard-working, senior citizen nomads made some readers understand the structural injustices in our nation. Recently I was perusing the Sunday New York Times Magazine and bumped into an article by Rachel del Valle titled Why Use a Dictionary in the Age of Internet Search. She defined dictionaries as field guides to the life of language. It was an analog that prompted me to read on. She went on to say that she owned a much-prized 1954 Webster’s New International Second Edition Dictionary, purchased some years ago on a street in New York City. It has 5,000 pages, the paper marbled India ink with a thumb index. Like a compelling sculpture, it has found a place on a table near her workspace, always opened, likely to the last word she looked up. I’ve owned countless dictionaries over the years, some dogeared paperbacks, others hard covered, the corners a bit frayed, often boxed up along with favored fiction when I moved, others lost or loaned. For a time, I owned the Oxford English Dictionary, which arrived in a two-volume set, accompanied by a magnifying glass; by the early 1800s the Oxford had some 400,000 entries, ever revised and added to. I confess that I love language, and relish coming across an esoteric word that appears like a stranger, unrecognizable, yet used with confidence in the context of a sentence. Often the meaning is elusive until the definition of that singular word is nailed down. An example would be the word “inchoate,” meaning “not fully formed or developed.” I doubt that I have ever used that word in conversation, or could pronounce it correctly. And for reasons that escape me, I can’t seem to hold its definition in memory. But there is something about inchoate that is interesting, even attractive in that category referred to as onomatopoeia – phonetically resembling the sound it describes (like oink or tick tock). If I still had my Oxford English Dictionary, I might even look up its derivation. An example offered by del Valle is “orrery,” which is defined as a mechanical model of our solar system used to represent relative positions and motions of our sun and planets. I can look at that word with admiration and try to quietly pronounce it, knowing I will never slip it into a sentence, written or spoken. But it stands at the ready, just in case. Del Valle compares finding such a word to prying open an oyster and finding a small pearl inside, or discovering a solvable mystery. Such words and their meaning do not exist in the realm of guesswork, for dictionaries are not arbiters of language nor do they create language – people do. And it’s people who swim in the stream of connotation and denotation, ever changing verbs into nouns, a most recent example being a simple word like “ask.” Still a verb, but now a favored noun, i.e. “that’s a big ask.” I’m tempted to say that encountering a newbie word is akin to a bird watcher spotting a rare species, one never seen before, requiring a field guide search, the excitement almost palpable. As a final note and in the interest of full disclosure: I first write all my copy by hand, (I favor ink on paper, in books and newspapers). And then, for the final edit, I turn to my MacBook Pro that possesses an image of a dictionary cum thesaurus with “Aa” on its cover, tucked into a long row of helpful guides, right next to Firefox. I use it repeatedly, on occasion glancing over at my opened dictionary with a sigh, trying to reject the idea that it is anachronistic, but still a useful cartography of our language. Apparently originating in the middle ages, historical interest groups at all levels of governments all over the world seem to have their own commemorative system of celebrating the connection of a location with a special event, person or structure. articles.text: I’m a witch, or, to keep with the preferred terminology, I practice witchcraft. Witchiness does not define me. That said, I’ve been a practicing witch since the Middle Ages, making me, I suppose, a middle-aged witch. I know of what I speak when I say that many of you have unpleasant misconceptions about us. I address them herewith. Myth 1 - Witches are ugly. I’m really surprised to hear this in our supposedly woke era. Our faces have character. We have strong features. Personally, I wouldn’t trust a woman who doesn’t have a large wart on the tip of her nose. A pointy chin and missing teeth proclaim our refusal to accept traditional ideas of beauty. Admittedly, none of us own mirrors. Myth 2 - Witches have green skin. No, it just looks that way when we stand under fluorescent light. No one looks good under fluorescent light. Myth 3 - Witches cackle. Such an ugly way of saying we enjoy a good laugh. While not everyone shares our sense of humor –I crack up seeing our neighbor’s livestock break out in boils after my shadow crosses their path, for example – we’re not the type to titter demurely behind a dainty fan. Deal with it. Myth 4 - Witches live in castles. Don’t I wish! More like a third-floor walkup with no view. Some of us are fortunate enough to live in a cooperative housing community, but you have to join a coven. Myth 5 - There are good witches and wicked witches. Is anyone really all good or all evil? Even a “good” witch might omit a spell-casting fee on her tax return, and a “wicked” witch might spend a quiet afternoon grooming her flying monkeys. Let’s drop the labels please. Myth 6 - Witches eat children. False! We used to eat children. We removed children from our diet in the late 1950s, early 1960s, when – coincidentally, I emphasize – the childhood obesity epidemic began. For a variety of reasons, and not just for our own health concerns, we witches as a group decided to forego excessive consumption of adipose tissue. The many benefits of our abstemious approach include being able to stay aloft longer on our brooms. Myth 7 - Witches construct gingerbread houses to lure children. I’ve already addressed the child-eating canard, but it should be obvious that gingerbread does not weather well. You can still find some pre-war lofts made of the stuff, but hipsters have remodeled them and stripped much of the ornaments that once made them so attractive to youngsters – not that yummy icing was ever intended to lure the little ones. And if people associate gingerbread houses with eating kids, why bake them as a Christmas treat? Weird. Myth 8 - Male witches are called warlocks. To outsiders, yes, but we refer to them as the men’s auxiliary to the witch community. Myth 9 - Witches always wear black. in Manhattan. You see that more with witches Myth 10 - Witches concoct poisons. We have recipes, just like any culturally distinct people. We slowcook them in simmering cauldrons using traditional ingredients, such as eyes of organic newts, toes of local frogs, and tongues of dogs (pure-bred only). Right now, we’re in our test kitchens developing dishes suitable for the general public. Here, try the soup … just a spoonful … that’s all you’ll need … for a nice, long sleep. Phil Witte, a Piedmont resident, is a humorist and a weekly cartoonist in the Piedmont Post with the single-panel cartoon, FLIP.

articles.text: Members of Walking on Wednesdays gather for a photo on Wednesday, October 8 at a home on La Salle Avenue. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group was surprised last Wednesday, October, to see a half dozen police officers at the Exedra, the starting location each Wednesday morning for the walkers. Was there a problem, they wondered? No. The Police Department was hosting another in their series of Coffee With a Cop events. Chief Jeremy Bowers welcomed the walkers and stressed the importance of community and how Piedmont benefits from it. A large group of 40 walkers were on hand for Part 2 of Hope Salzer’s tours of Healthy Landscapes Front Gardens sponsored by Piedmont Connect. Hope had taken the walkers to three gardens the prior Wednesday, and the walkers wanted to see more. Piedmont Connect is a community organization supporting efforts to build a sustainable future. The plan for the day was for Hope to take the walkers to four new gardens, starting at 250 La Salle Avenue, a unique, steep, natural garden, with every inch packed with “succession planting” vegetation that provides color throughout the year. Additionally, all these plants absorb rain better than grass would (if we ever get rain again), reducing excessive runoff down the steep yard to the house. Even the strip from the curb to the front of the garden is covered with plants. The yard supports birds, insects, and other wildlife, but has also survived the deer that roam throughout the neighborhood. The next stop was 131 La Salle with a different type of drought tolerant garden. It is more formally structured, and currently has vibrant, early fall red and yellow colors from bottle brush, firecracker, and other plants. It was noted that former Piedmont mayor and landscape designer Valerie Matzger designed the yard for the homeowner. There is a permeable walkway and other surfaces that allow rain to soak into the ground. The environmental mindset of the owner was further evidenced by solar panels on the roof. The home’s front steps provided tiers for the walkers to pose for the attached group photo. The group continued to 66 La Salle where a new garden was planted this past spring, and shows how quickly a lovely, drought tolerant garden can be created. This was another steeply sloped front garden of a home above the creek on St. James that also survives the foraging of local deer. The garden has many plants that attract bees for their pollen and nectar. Hope stressed the importance of all types of bees and the need to protect them. She told the group they are in real danger. In fact, the bumble bee has been recently named an endangered species. Birds are also being harmed by human actions, and their population is in decline. This garden uses drip irrigation and includes a colorful flower named Salvia “Hot Lips.” Asked about the ground covering, Hope explained her preference for using compost. She said the challenge is getting enough of it to cover a garden. Piedmont residents can get quantities of compost from Republic Services, the city’s trash removal and recycling service. The last garden was at 98 Sea View Avenue, another beautifully designed and lovingly maintained garden with a large variety of plants, flowers, and small trees. There are manzanita, citrus, climbing roses, native grasses, and many more. Succession planting provides color throughout the year and highly efficient drip irrigation minimizes water usage. While they were there, the owner came out and told the walkers how he has maintained the yard, and how much he enjoys it. Before the parade of walkers made their way back to the Exedra, they gave Hope a big round of applause. Everyone was impressed with her knowledge and passion for environmental sustainability. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: • The Rhone River wine growing region in France is divided into two halves – the north and the south. They could not be more different. The South is huge and produces oceans of wine – a lot of it cheap Cotes du Rhone, yet it also has some heavyweight appellations like Chateauneuf du Pape, Gigondas and Vacqueras. The main red grape is Grenache with lots of Mourvedre, Carignanne and Syrah grown. By comparison the Northern Rhone region is tiny and it stars only one red grape – Syrah. For whites, Viognier is king. with some Marsanne and Roussanne grown. Being from California, my wine palate was developed on Zinfandel, Cabernet, Pinot Noir and Petite Sirah. As much as I still love those varietals, I must say I have fallen in love with the Northern Rhone. These days I rarely get more satisfaction than opening a bottle of Viognier from the Condrieu AVA or a Syrah from Cote Rotie, Hermitage or St. Joseph. While California makes some great Syrahs, too many of them become heavy and ponderous, lacking balance and acidity. And as for Viognier, I have had many California examples, but I have yet to find anything close to the magic of Condrieu. I was thrilled to have the opportunity recently to evaluate the wines of one of the Northern Rhone’s premier producer, Francois Villard. His wines have tremendous perfume and are exquisitely balanced and refreshing. I also appreciate that in a world where wine prices have gone absolutely crazy, Villard has held the line; his wines represent great values. The wines are imported in the U.S. by Jack Edwards Selections, a Napa based firm that specializes in small, high-quality producers from France. You can check out their other portfolio wines at www.jackedwardscollection.com. 2018 Francois Villard Les Contours de Deponcins Viognier, $19.99 (Great Value) This is a “baby Condrieu” made from Viognier vines planted outside the official boundaries of Condrieu. It comes close to its daddy and is a good value to boot. It has a lovely jasmine nose with tasty pear and apricot fruit Francois Villard Francois Villard is one of the up-and-coming bright lights in the Rhone Valley. After previous careers as a chef and sommelier, he ventured into wine growing in 1991 with a small parcel of vines in Condrieu, He has since expanded it into holdings in Cote Rotie. Villard’s style has evolved from the big, heavy oak-laden style of wines that were popular in the 90’s (and still are with Guigal) to more elegant finesse-style wines attained by short fermentations with mostly full clusters. articles.text: Swim Across America event a major fundraiser for cardiology, cancer Bob Tandler (left), Levy Gerzberg, Josh Bernstein, and Peter Gertler celebrate after completing the swim in the annual Golden Gate Invitational on October 2. Last weekend in San Francisco Bay, intrepid swimmers from all over the United States converged to raise money for UCSF. On Saturday, October 2, Dr. Josh Bernstein hosted his annual Golden Gate Invitational Swim to benefit the UCSF Cardiology Council. Chief of Cardiology, Dr. Carlin Long, spoke to the 28 swimmers beforehand about the importance of their fundraising efforts, which raised thousands of dollars. However, the infamous San Francisco fog didn’t cooperate, and Bernstein called for Plan B on the morning of the swim, changing the route to a swim from Alcatraz to Aquatic Park. The swimmers all took the change in stride. Then, on Sunday hundreds of swimmers gathered on the beach at St Francis Yacht Club to swim to Aquatic Park for UCSF Pediatric Cancer research and treatment. Bernstein swam again, this time as a member of the team of 3-time cancer survivor Susan Helmrich, “Team Susan Survives.” Team Susan raised over $135,000 of the more than half a million dollars raised on Sunday. “For those of us who love swimming, it’s a pleasure to raise money for such worthy causes, even when the water in the Bay is chilly,” he said. Josh Bernstein and Susan Helmrich in San Francisco Bay at the Golden Gate Invitational Swim. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

Cheryl, whose background is in that design niche, founded this podcast to have conversations with female interior designers about creating nourishing, healing spaces in clients’ homes, especially in light of what the collective has been going through in this time of Covid. If you know me, you know I love to “go deep or go home.” Cheryl asked me some very compelling questions. I shared about my military family’s tumultuous history (“If you pull up a carrot every time it starts to grow, you don’t have a full carrot”), and how that inspired my desire to become an interior designer and have an impact on the experience of home for others. Ultimately, my life transformed exponentially when I realized that what matters is our connection to Self, higher power, Source, whatever you want to call it. If we aren’t connected to that, we will never feel at home, no matter how beautiful our spaces are. As a beauty maker, my primary desire is to facilitate, inspire, invite people to see this.
